questions.stem: A nurse is developing a discharge plan for a client with limited access to transportation and unstable housing, and a colleague suggests these issues are outside the nurse's role to address. Addressing these factors as part of the discharge plan reflects an understanding of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Concerns considered relevant mainly to social workers, with fairly little meaningful nursing role involved, as the colleague suggested","B":"Social determinants of health, which significantly influence a client's ability to manage their health after discharge","C":"Factors that are generally understood to be unrelated to a client's overall health outcomes after leaving the hospital","D":"Issues that fall largely outside the recognized scope of professional nursing practice, as the colleague suggested"}}
questions.rationale: Social determinants of health — including factors like housing stability, transportation access, income, and education — significantly influence health outcomes and a client's ability to follow a care plan. Nurses play an important role in identifying and addressing these factors, often in collaboration with social work and other resources.
questions.source_name: Healthy People 2030 — Social Determinants of Health Framework
questions.source_detail: Impact of Social Determinants on Health Outcomes

questions.stem: A pregnant client at 32 weeks gestation has a blood pressure of 148/94 mmHg on two occasions four hours apart, new-onset proteinuria, and now reports a new headache and visual spots. The nurse should recognize this combination as consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Preeclampsia, given the blood pressure findings, proteinuria, and new headache and visual changes together","B":"Normal pregnancy-related blood pressure changes, despite the proteinuria and new neurological symptoms described","C":"Chronic hypertension unrelated to pregnancy, despite the new proteinuria and neurological symptoms appearing now","D":"Gestational diabetes, a condition that would not explain this client's blood pressure or neurological findings"}}
questions.rationale: ACOG diagnostic criteria for preeclampsia include new-onset blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg on two occasions at least four hours apart after 20 weeks gestation, combined with new-onset proteinuria (or other signs of end-organ involvement in the absence of proteinuria).
questions.source_name: ACOG — Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia Practice Bulletin

questions.stem: A pregnant client at 34 weeks gestation with a known posterior placenta reports sudden, painless, bright red vaginal bleeding, and the fetal heart rate remains reassuring. The nurse should recognize this presentation as most consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Placental abruption, a condition that would more classically present with painful bleeding and uterine tenderness rather than this painless pattern","B":"Normal Braxton Hicks contractions, which would not explain the vaginal bleeding described","C":"A urinary tract infection, a condition that would not explain this pattern of vaginal bleeding","D":"Placenta previa, a diagnosis matching this exact clinical picture of painless, vivid vaginal bleeding late in pregnancy"}}
questions.rationale: Painless, bright red vaginal bleeding in the second half of pregnancy is the classic presentation of placenta previa, in contrast to placental abruption, which typically presents with painful, dark red bleeding and a rigid, tender abdomen.
questions.source_name: Merck Manual — Placenta Previa Clinical Presentation
questions.source_detail: Painless Bright Red Bleeding as Hallmark of Placenta Previa

questions.stem: A multiparous client in labor progresses from 4 cm to complete cervical dilation within one hour, with intense, frequent contractions, and the nurse notes the fetal head is now visible at the perineum. The nurse should recognize this as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Precipitous labor, requiring close monitoring for maternal and fetal complications given how rapidly labor has progressed","B":"A normal, expected labor progression pattern that requires no additional monitoring beyond routine care","C":"A clear indication to delay all delivery preparations until further notice, despite the visible fetal head","D":"A sign that the client's labor has actually stopped progressing, despite the rapid dilation and visible fetal head"}}
questions.rationale: Precipitous labor refers to an unusually rapid labor and delivery, often completing within three hours or less from onset of contractions to birth. It requires close monitoring for potential complications, including uterine rupture, cervical/vaginal lacerations, and fetal distress.
questions.source_name: Standard Obstetric Nursing References — Precipitous Labor
questions.source_detail: Recognition and Monitoring of Precipitous Labor

questions.stem: A newborn is assessed at 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth using the Apgar scoring system. This assessment primarily evaluates:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The mother's own postpartum recovery status, rather than any newborn-specific finding","B":"Only the newborn's estimated gestational age at the time of birth","C":"Only the newborn's recorded birth weight, with no other parameter assessed","D":"The newborn's heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability, and color"}}
questions.rationale: The Apgar score evaluates five components at 1 and 5 minutes after birth: heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability, and color, each scored 0-2, providing a quick assessment of the newborn's immediate transition to extrauterine life.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Apgar Score Guidelines

questions.stem: A client presents with fever, severe headache, photophobia, and nuchal rigidity, and a family member mentions the client was fine just yesterday. The nurse should suspect:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Meningitis, requiring urgent evaluation given this classic combination of findings and rapid onset","B":"A tension headache, a condition that would not typically produce fever or nuchal rigidity","C":"A normal viral illness requiring only rest, despite the nuchal rigidity and photophobia described","D":"Migraine without further concern, despite the fever and nuchal rigidity present in this client"}}
questions.rationale: Fever, severe headache, photophobia, and nuchal rigidity are classic signs of meningitis, an infection/inflammation of the meninges that requires urgent evaluation (including lumbar puncture) and prompt treatment, given the risk of serious complications.
questions.source_name: CDC — Meningitis Clinical Signs and Symptoms

questions.stem: A teenage male presents with sudden, severe unilateral scrotal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The nurse should recognize this as a possible surgical emergency requiring:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Managed conservatively at home initially, since this type of pain often subsides within a few days","B":"Immediate evaluation, since testicular torsion has a limited window (typically about 6 hours) for testicular salvage","C":"Managed with scheduled outpatient follow-up, provided oral analgesics adequately control the pain","D":"Managed with local heat application, since warmth is believed to improve blood flow to the area"}}
questions.rationale: Sudden, severe unilateral testicular pain with nausea/vomiting is the classic presentation of testicular torsion, a surgical emergency. Testicular salvage rates are highest when surgery occurs within about 6 hours of symptom onset, making immediate evaluation and treatment critical.
questions.source_name: AAFP — Testicular Torsion Diagnosis and Management

questions.stem: A client with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia reports lower abdominal pain, an inability to void for several hours, and the nurse notes a palpable, distended bladder on assessment. The nurse should recognize this as consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Normal bladder fullness that would be expected to resolve without any nursing intervention","B":"A straightforward urinary tract infection, a diagnosis that would not fully explain the inability to void","C":"Acute urinary retention, requiring prompt intervention such as catheterization, especially given this client's BPH history","D":"Expected findings typically observed shortly after a client has voided normally, despite the client's inability to void"}}
questions.rationale: Lower abdominal pain, inability to void, and a palpable, distended bladder are classic signs of acute urinary retention, which requires prompt intervention (often catheterization) to relieve the obstruction and prevent complications such as bladder injury or renal impairment.
questions.source_name: Clinical Urology References — Acute Urinary Retention Recognition and Management
questions.source_detail: Signs and Symptoms of Acute Urinary Retention

questions.stem: A client develops a severe systemic allergic-type reaction after receiving IV contrast dye, without prior sensitization or an IgE-mediated mechanism. The nurse understands this reaction is managed similarly to true anaphylaxis because:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Managed with supportive observation alone in most cases, since the mechanism does not involve a true IgE-mediated allergic process","B":"Expected to remain confined to cutaneous symptoms such as hives, without meaningful risk of airway or hemodynamic compromise developing","C":"Considered unlikely to occur on a client's first exposure, since prior sensitization is generally thought to be required for this type of reaction","D":"The clinical presentation and life-threatening risk are similar, so emergency management (including epinephrine) follows the same general approach"}}
questions.rationale: Although the precise immunologic mechanism may differ (non-IgE-mediated reactions were previously termed "anaphylactoid"), the clinical presentation and life-threatening potential are similar to true anaphylaxis, so emergency management, including prompt epinephrine administration, generally follows the same approach.
questions.source_name: World Allergy Organization — Anaphylaxis Guidance

questions.stem: A nurse is monitoring a fetal heart rate tracing during labor. The normal baseline fetal heart rate range is generally considered to be:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"180-220 beats per minute","B":"60-80 beats per minute","C":"40-60 beats per minute","D":"110-160 beats per minute"}}
questions.rationale: The normal baseline fetal heart rate is generally 110-160 beats per minute. Rates outside this range (bradycardia below 110 or tachycardia above 160) warrant further assessment and may indicate fetal compromise depending on the full clinical picture.
questions.source_name: ACOG / NICHD — Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Normal Baseline Fetal Heart Rate Range

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a healthy newborn shortly after birth. Which heart rate finding would be considered within the normal newborn range?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"140 beats per minute","B":"250 beats per minute","C":"30 beats per minute","D":"50 beats per minute"}}
questions.rationale: The normal newborn heart rate range is generally about 110-160 beats per minute (with some sources citing up to 180 during crying), significantly higher than typical adult ranges. A rate of 140 beats per minute falls within this normal range.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Newborn Assessment Guidelines

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing vital signs for a 2-year-old child. The nurse understands that normal pediatric vital sign ranges:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Lower than adult norms for most parameters, most notably respiratory rate, which tends to run below adult values","B":"Comparable to adult norms once a child reaches approximately 2 years of age, per standard pediatric references","C":"Interpreted using the same baseline expectations applied to an adult of similar body size","D":"Vary significantly by age, with higher normal heart and respiratory rates in younger children compared to adults"}}
questions.rationale: Normal vital sign ranges vary significantly by age in pediatric clients, with younger children generally having higher normal heart rates and respiratory rates compared to adults, gradually approaching adult norms as the child grows older.
questions.source_name: Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) — Age-Based Vital Sign Norms
questions.source_detail: Age-Related Variation in Pediatric Vital Signs

questions.stem: A client with suspected deep vein thrombosis has an elevated D-dimer level, and the nurse is preparing to discuss next steps with the client, who asks if this confirms the diagnosis. The nurse understands this finding:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Is considered sufficient on its own to fully establish a diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis without needing any further imaging test done","B":"Is a nonspecific marker suggesting possible clot formation or breakdown, meaning further diagnostic testing such as ultrasound is still needed to confirm DVT","C":"Reflects a process largely separate from the body's usual coagulation and fibrinolysis pathways altogether in most clients","D":"Is low enough here to make a diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis considerably less likely overall for this particular client"}}
questions.rationale: D-dimer is a nonspecific marker of fibrin degradation that can be elevated in DVT, pulmonary embolism, and many other conditions (infection, pregnancy, recent surgery). An elevated D-dimer supports further diagnostic testing (such as Doppler ultrasound) but does not confirm DVT on its own; a normal D-dimer has higher value in ruling out DVT in low-risk clients.
questions.source_name: Clinical Laboratory Reference Standards — D-Dimer Testing
questions.source_detail: D-Dimer as a Nonspecific Clotting Marker

questions.stem: A client's erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is significantly elevated. The nurse understands this nonspecific finding suggests:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The presence of an inflammatory process somewhere in the body","B":"Consistent with entirely normal, unremarkable systemic metabolic function","C":"Specifically diagnostic of an underlying pneumonia infection on its own","D":"A finding consistent with improved, strengthened overall immune function"}}
questions.rationale: ESR is a nonspecific marker of inflammation, similar to CRP, that can be elevated in infection, autoimmune conditions, malignancy, and other inflammatory states. It supports clinical assessment but does not identify a specific diagnosis on its own.
questions.source_name: Clinical Laboratory Reference Standards — Inflammatory Markers
questions.source_detail: ESR as a Nonspecific Inflammatory Marker

questions.stem: A nurse is calculating a 1-minute Apgar score for a newborn with a heart rate over 100 bpm, strong cry, active movement, grimace/cough with stimulation, and a body that is pink with blue hands and feet. Which score should the nurse assign specifically for the color component?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"1 point, reflecting a body that is pink with blue extremities (acrocyanosis), a common finding immediately after birth","B":"Color is not actually one of the five categories included in the standard Apgar scoring system","C":"2 points, a score that would require the newborn to be fully pink over the entire body, including the hands and feet","D":"0 points, a score that would require the newborn to appear blue or pale over the entire body, not just the extremities"}}
questions.rationale: In the Apgar scoring system, color is scored 0 (blue/pale all over), 1 (body pink with blue extremities — acrocyanosis, a common and often normal finding shortly after birth), or 2 (completely pink). A newborn with a pink body and blue extremities receives a score of 1 for color.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Apgar Score Components and Scoring

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a new parent about umbilical cord care for their newborn. Which instruction is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Sponge-bathed rather than fully submerged, until the cord stump has completely separated on its own","B":"Covered loosely with a breathable dressing until the stump shows early signs of detachment","C":"Keep the cord stump clean and dry, allowing it to air dry, and fold diapers below the cord to avoid irritation","D":"Left in place until it separates on its own, with gentle traction applied only if it appears nearly detached"}}
questions.rationale: Standard newborn cord care involves keeping the stump clean and dry, allowing air exposure, avoiding submersion baths until the cord falls off naturally (typically 1-3 weeks), and folding diapers below the stump to prevent irritation and contamination, allowing natural separation.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Newborn Umbilical Cord Care

questions.stem: A nurse is providing perineal care instructions to a postpartum client. Which instruction is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Apply ice directly to the perineum without a protective barrier or cloth between the ice and skin","B":"Wipe from front to back, and use a peri-bottle with warm water after voiding to promote comfort and hygiene","C":"Avoid all perineal hygiene entirely for the first week postpartum to protect the healing tissue","D":"Wipe from back to front after voiding or defecating, then pat the area dry with a clean towel"}}
questions.rationale: Postpartum perineal care includes wiping front to back to reduce infection risk, and using a peri-bottle with warm water after voiding or defecating to gently cleanse the area and promote comfort, particularly important with any perineal trauma or episiotomy.
questions.source_name: AWHONN — Postpartum Perineal Care Guidelines

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client in the third trimester of pregnancy who is lying supine for an ultrasound and suddenly reports dizziness, lightheadedness, and nausea. The nurse's priority action is to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Reposition the client onto her left side to relieve pressure the gravid uterus is placing on the vena cava","B":"Encourage the client to sit up rapidly, reasoning that the dizziness is unrelated to her current supine positioning","C":"Elevate only the client's legs while keeping her positioned flat on her back throughout the procedure","D":"Have the client remain flat on her back and simply wait for the symptoms to resolve on their own"}}
questions.rationale: In late pregnancy, the gravid uterus can compress the inferior vena cava when a client lies supine, reducing venous return and causing supine hypotensive syndrome. Repositioning to the left lateral position relieves this pressure and is the priority intervention.
questions.source_name: ACOG — Maternal Positioning in Pregnancy
questions.source_detail: Supine Hypotensive Syndrome and Left Lateral Positioning

questions.stem: When giving a bed bath to a client, the nurse should generally wash the body in which order?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"From the feet upward to the face, working against the usual clean-to-dirty sequence","B":"From the cleanest area (such as the face) to the least clean area (such as the perineal area) last","C":"In a random order based on staff convenience, with no particular clean-to-dirty sequence","D":"From the perineal area first, then moving upward to wash the face at the very end"}}
questions.rationale: Standard bed bath technique follows a clean-to-dirty principle, generally starting with the face/eyes (cleanest area) and moving toward the perineal area (least clean) last, using separate sections of the washcloth or fresh water as needed to minimize cross-contamination.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Bed Bath Technique

questions.stem: A nurse is providing postpartum follow-up care six weeks after delivery and screens the client for depression using a validated tool, even though the client reports feeling "basically fine." This practice reflects:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A screening that is considered most relevant during pregnancy itself, with frequency typically decreasing after delivery","B":"A screening best deferred to a mental health specialist rather than incorporated into routine postpartum nursing visits like this one","C":"A lower-priority screening, since most postpartum mood changes are assumed to resolve without any formal intervention","D":"Standard, recommended practice at this stage of care, since low mood may not be obvious even when someone reports feeling okay, and early support matters"}}
questions.rationale: Routine screening for postpartum depression using validated tools (such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale) is a recommended standard practice, since postpartum depression is common, often underrecognized, and benefits significantly from timely identification and treatment.
questions.source_name: ACOG — Screening for Perinatal Depression
